evidence: Cic. Fam. 9.3.1: quod velle tē putō
terms.comment: With an accusative and infinitive. In Cicero’s letters putō also stands alone as an aside, “I think”; Nōn putāram is “I never thought of that” (Cic. Off. 1.81).

evidence: Cic. Tusc. 1.92: nōndum, opīnor, est experrēctus
terms.comment: Most often as an aside, opīnor or ut opīnor, “I think”, “I suppose”. For Sīc opīnor see I think so.

evidence: Cic. Att. 13.49.1: quam equidem rūrī esse arbitror
terms.comment: A considered judgement; also as an aside, ut arbitror.

terms.gloss: think, be of the opinion; think it best
evidence: Cic. de Or. 2.367: surgendum cēnseō et requiēscendum
terms.comment: Quid cēnsēs? asks “What do you think?”; with a gerundive it gives advice: surgendum cēnseō, I think we should get up.

phrases.latin: hoc salsum esse putās? fugit tē, inepte
phrases.english: You think that’s funny? You’ve got it wrong, silly.

phrases.latin: quid ergō potissimum scrībam? quod velle tē putō, citō mē ad tē esse ventūrum
phrases.english: So what shall I write above all? What I think you want: that I’ll be with you soon.

phrases.latin: nec committere, ut aliquandō dīcendum sit: Nōn putāram.
phrases.english: and not to let it come to having to say, “I never thought of that.”
